planting.note: Mount on cork bark or tree fern fiber, or pot in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic orchid mix; grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant with high humidity in zone 9, since Bulbophyllum medusae cannot tolerate frost.

directions: Grow in bright indirect to moderate shade with high humidity, mounted on cork bark or tree fern fiber, or potted in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic orchid mix. Medusa Orchid takes its dramatic common name from its extraordinary flower spike, which bears a dense cluster of long, extremely fine, pale cream to yellow-green threadlike petals that dangle and sway like a mass of hair or tentacles, unlike any typical orchid flower shape. The unusual bloom has a faint, somewhat unpleasant fragrance characteristic of many Bulbophyllum species, which are frequently pollinated by flies rather than bees. Like other epiphytic bulbophyllums it grows from small pseudobulbs along a creeping rhizome and spreads slowly across its mount over time. Keep humidity high and water regularly without letting the mount or mix stay soggy, since good air movement and drainage are essential to prevent rot.

common_name: Hooded Lady of the Night Orchid (Brassavola Cucullata)

planting.note: Mount on cork bark or pot in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic orchid mix; grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in bright light in zone 9, since Brassavola cucullata cannot tolerate frost.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light to a few hours of gentle direct sun, mounted on cork bark or potted in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic orchid mix that dries between waterings. Brassavola cucullata, a relative of the popular Brassavola nodosa, has similarly narrow, cylindrical, succulent leaves adapted to store water through dry spells, but produces spidery, narrow-petaled greenish-yellow flowers with a distinctive fringed, hood-shaped lip. Like its relative, its flowers release an intense, sweet fragrance almost exclusively at night, when it is pollinated by moths in its native range from Mexico through South America. Water thoroughly then let the mount or mix approach dryness before watering again, since good drainage and air movement around the roots are essential to prevent rot in this epiphytic species.

common_name: Skinner's Cattleya (National Flower of Costa Rica)

planting.note: Mount on cork bark or pot in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic orchid mix; grow as a houseplant or shaded patio plant in bright light in zone 9, since Cattleya skinneri cannot tolerate frost.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light to a few hours of gentle direct sun in a coarse, fast-draining epiphytic orchid mix of bark and perlite, letting the mix approach dryness between thorough waterings. Cattleya skinneri, the national flower of Costa Rica, produces clusters of large, showy, rose-purple flowers with a deeper magenta, ruffled lip in spring, held above sturdy, upright pseudobulbs topped with a pair of leathery leaves typical of the genus. Its reliable spring bloom and classic cattleya form and fragrance have made it a long-favorite species among orchid collectors, valued both for cut flowers historically and as a garden or greenhouse specimen. Provide strong, bright light for the best flowering, since cattleyas grown in too much shade produce lush foliage but few flowers, and allow a slight drying period between waterings to mimic natural conditions and discourage rot.
